implementation_notes: Each JDK context carries its own map: Optional.map applies the mapper only when a value is present and returns an empty Optional otherwise (documented as returning 'an Optional describing (as if by ofNullable) the result of applying the given mapping function to the value'), and Stream.map applies it to every element of a lazy pipeline that runs only when a terminal operation is reached. Java has no higher-kinded types, so there is no Functor type to implement: generic code either works against one concrete context or adopts a Kind<F, A> encoding from a library. The naming is per context (map for Optional/Stream, thenApply for CompletableFuture), which is why the abstraction stays a convention in Java; a hand-written generic interface is justified only when several contexts must share one helper.
code_sketch:
Optional<String> host = config.map(Config::host);    // empty stays empty

List<String> names = people.stream()
    .map(Person::name)                 // lazy: nothing runs yet
    .toList();                         // terminal operation

// no HKT: a shared helper is written per context or against Kind<F, A>
pitfalls: Optional.map wraps its result with ofNullable: a mapper that returns null silently turns a present value into an empty Optional.
Stream.map is lazy and single-use: nothing runs without a terminal operation, and reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException.

Checked exceptions do not fit java.util.function.Function: a throwing mapper needs a try/catch inside the lambda or an unchecked wrapper, and the failure then surfaces at the terminal operation rather than at the map.

variants.name: thenApply over CompletableFuture (map inside an asynchronous context)
variants.implementation_notes: The asynchronous context maps with thenApply: the Javadoc defines it as returning a new CompletionStage that, when the stage completes normally, is 'executed with this stage's result as the argument to the supplied function', and states explicitly that the method 'is analogous to Optional.map and Stream.map' - the same operation in a different context. Failures are structure-preserving for free: a stage that completes exceptionally leaves fn uninvoked and the derived future failed, which is what a lawful map owes. Use thenApplyAsync with an explicit executor when the mapping function blocks or must not run on the completing thread, and thenCompose when the mapping function itself returns a future.
pitfalls: thenApply runs on whatever thread completed the previous stage (often a pool or I/O thread): blocking work there stalls unrelated completions - move it to thenApplyAsync with an explicit executor.
Exceptions inside the mapper are wrapped in CompletionException and surface at the consumer (join/get), not at the thenApply call, so error handling has to be attached to the derived stage.
A mapper that returns a future nests the context (CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<B>>); thenCompose is the bind that flattens it.
